causalModel.founding: The Border road was laid on a Dunmer line from Stormhold to Thorn. Below Greenspring the road meets the river marsh and an inlet stream. The keepers of the road carry it over both on piled timber.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: The road runs along the dry strip at the mountain foot. It crosses water only at the points where the dry ground gives out. The two crossings are at the inlet mouth and at one reach of the river marsh.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: The crossings have no residents. The village above keeps the planks. The trade of the village goes out along this road.
causalModel.pressures: The piles rot in the marsh within a few seasons. The village above has to keep replacing the piles.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: A stone causeway would replace the planks if a payer funded one.

districts.notes: The stretch of the Border road from the Greenspring track west to the river marsh, with its two plank crossings and the timber stair up the river bank.

why.what: The district is the Border road between the Greenspring track and the river marsh. It holds two plank crossings, the timber stair and the marks beside the way.
why.whyHere: The road runs along the dry strip at the mountain foot. It has to cross water twice before it can climb the river bank.
why.whyNeighbours: Greenspring stands up its own track at the east end. The road runs on west toward Stormhold.
why.playerPurpose: The road is the way between Greenspring and the west. It is dry underfoot only where the planks carry it.
why.microGeography: The ground is firm lowland and bank between black marsh water. The road is a worn earth strip on the dry ground.

parcels.orientationWhy: The planks are laid north to south along the line of the road. They end in line with the stair up the bank. They end 0.4 m short of the foot of the stair.

why.what: The river crossing is plank spans on piles. The spans carry the road over a reach of the river marsh. They run up to the foot of the timber stair.
why.whyHere: The road meets the river marsh at its narrowest reach. The water stands about 1.3 m deep.
why.whySpot: The crossing runs from the dry ground at the north end. It runs straight south across the marsh to the foot of the stair up the bank.
why.whyNeighbours: A cairn and a grave mound stand at the north head of the crossing. The timber stair climbs the bank from the south end of the crossing.
why.playerPurpose: The crossing carries the road across the river marsh. It is dry underfoot from the cairn to the stair.
why.microGeography: The planks stand a hand's breadth over black marsh water. They rest on sunk piles.

parcels.orientationWhy: The stair climbs south on the line of the planks. A walker crosses the 0.4 m gap from the last span onto the bottom tread. A walker steps off the top tread onto the bank top.

why.what: The stair is a steep timber stair of three flights. It carries the road from the river crossing up the river bank.
why.whyHere: The bank face is 7.85 m high over 2 m of ground at the south end of the crossing. The bank is too steep to walk or to cut back.
why.whySpot: The stair stands at the south end of the planks. There the road leaves the marsh and climbs onto the bank.
why.whyNeighbours: The planks of the river crossing end at the foot of the stair. The road runs on along the top of the bank.
why.playerPurpose: The stair carries the road up the bank. A walker climbs step by step from the planks to the dry ground.
why.microGeography: The foot of the stair is sunk in the marsh mud 0.4 m past the planks. The stair leans up the face of the bank. Its top tread meets the grass at the bank edge.

parcels.orientationWhy: The inlet deck is laid east-south-east along the line of the road. It runs straight across the inlet mouth between two dry banks.

why.what: The inlet deck is plank spans on piles. The spans cross the mouth of the inlet stream.
why.whyHere: The inlet stream spreads into marsh at its mouth. The water is up to 1.07 m deep across the line of the road.
why.whySpot: The deck runs east from the dry ground below the bank. It crosses the mouth to the dry ground under the Greenspring rise.
why.whyNeighbours: A cairn marks the west head of the deck. The track up to Greenspring turns off a short walk to the east.
why.playerPurpose: The deck carries the road across the inlet mouth. It is the last wet stretch before Greenspring.
why.microGeography: The planks stand about a metre over the black water of the inlet mouth. They rest on sunk piles.

parcels.orientationWhy: A cairn and a totem stand on the verge. The verge is where the track comes down to the road.

why.what: The end of the road at Greenspring has a stone cairn and a tribe totem at the track head. A few loose rocks lie on the verge toward the inlet.
why.whyHere: The people of Greenspring keep this stretch. The verge is clear and the marks stand upright.
why.whySpot: The marks stand beside the track head. They stand off the road on the uphill side.
why.whyNeighbours: Greenspring lies up the track. The inlet deck is a short walk west.
why.playerPurpose: The marks show a walker where the track to Greenspring leaves the road.
why.microGeography: The ground is dry at the mountain foot. It is firm underfoot.

parcels.orientationWhy: A cold fire ring lies on the flat above the inlet. Rocks lie along both bends of the bank road. A cairn stands at the west head of the inlet deck.

why.what: The bank road runs between the two crossings. It has rocks at the bends and a cold fire ring above the inlet where travellers stop. A cairn stands at the head of the inlet deck.
why.whyHere: Greenspring maintains the plank crossings. Greenspring leaves the bank road between the crossings unkept. Fallen rocks lie on the bank road where they dropped. A cairn stands at the head of the inlet deck.
why.whySpot: The fire ring stands on flat ground above the inlet. The road levels out there before the deck.
why.whyNeighbours: The steps down to the river crossing lie west of the fire ring. The inlet deck lies east of the fire ring.
why.playerPurpose: The fire ring is cold. Travellers can rest at it between the two crossings.
why.microGeography: The ground is firm lowland on the bank top. The road is a worn earth strip.

parcels.orientationWhy: The cairn stands beside the north end of the river crossing. A grave mound lies on the flat ground beside the cairn.

why.what: A stone cairn stands at the north end of the river crossing. A low grave mound lies on the flat ground beside the cairn. Wet rocks lie at both ends of the planks.
why.whyHere: The road reaches the river marsh at this spot. The cairn shows a walker from the west where the planks begin.
why.whySpot: The cairn stands on the dry verge beside the first plank.
why.whyNeighbours: The river crossing runs south from the cairn to the timber stair.
why.playerPurpose: The cairn marks the start of the crossing for anyone coming from Stormhold. The grave mound shows that a traveller died on this stretch.
why.microGeography: The cairn stands at the edge of the marsh. Dry ground meets black water there.

routes.why: A few steps of trodden ground lead from the road to the cairn. The cairn stands at the track head.
Trodden ground leads from the road to the cold fire ring. Travellers stop at the fire ring at the bend.
A few steps of trodden ground lead from the road to the cairn. The cairn stands at the head of the river crossing.

approaches.sequence: The approach runs down the track from Greenspring. A cairn and a totem mark where the track meets the road. West along the road, the planks of the inlet deck show low over the marsh.
approaches.wayfinding: The road runs west from the track head. The road runs down to the inlet deck and on to the river crossing.

approaches.sequence: The approach runs south-east along the road from Stormhold. A cairn marks the head of the river crossing. The planks run straight across the marsh to a steep timber stair.
approaches.wayfinding: The way goes across the planks, up the stair and along the top of the bank.

networkTerminals.why: The road from Stormhold reaches the north end of the river crossing.
The Greenspring track meets the road at its east end.

combatSpaces.why: The flat top of the river bank lies between the steps and the inlet. It is the single open footing between the two crossings.

scaleGrounding.loreSource: The lore source is the route record route.road.stormhold-thorn. The route record describes the road as worn, with long timber bridges patched. The second source is world/sources/routes/route-structure-exemplars.json.
scaleGrounding.why: The place is a stretch of road. It has two plank crossings, a timber stair and road marks. The stretch has no residents.

candidates.why: The Border road below Greenspring crosses two marsh reaches. The crossing record bands both reaches as spans. crossing.major.009 is 36 m long and 1.32 m deep. crossing.major.012 is 26.4 m long and up to 1.07 m deep. The road climbs the river bank on a recorded stair. The road meets the built village's track. The stretch holds a bridge, a deck and a stair. No other place's ground lies on this stretch.
The candidate is the Blackwood Road from Claywater Station east to the Greenditch stairs.
candidates.rejectedBecause: Claywater already built the crossings on the Blackwood Road as fords and a ferry. The Blackwood Road needs no bridge or deck. Five unbuilt places hold the ground beside its stairs. The five places are Cartwright's Cross, Fort Greenditch, the Ridge-runners' Post, the Ashen Tower and the Drowned Embankment.
